grimoire.title: Venue power outage
grimoire.text: Switch to emergency lighting, keep stairwells clear, do not use elevators, account for every attendee by sector, check life-safety systems, coordinate with building management.

grimoire.title: Cloud region outage runbook
grimoire.text: Confirm on the provider status page, freeze deploys, fail over to a healthy region, shed non-critical load, post a customer status update every 30 minutes, open a postmortem.

grimoire.title: Flash flood
grimoire.text: Move to higher floors, cut power to flooded areas, never drive through water, stage pumps, track river gauges and official warnings.

grimoire.title: Fire / smoke evacuation
grimoire.text: Pull the alarm, evacuate via nearest stairwell, never elevators, assemble at the muster point, sweep sectors, report missing persons to fire services.

grimoire.title: Medical emergency at an event
grimoire.text: Call emergency services, send someone to fetch the AED, clear space, guide responders from the entrance, keep a log of times.

grimoire.title: Doctrine: EVACUATE
grimoire.text: Evacuate when the threat is mobile, there is structural compromise, or civilians are in the contact zone (pinned, trapped, exposed). Clear floors top-down and confirm empty.

snippets:
# The 28-Hour Meltdown: What Happened When AWS US-EAST-1 Overheated
A breakdown of the 28-hour aws us-east-1 outage in may 2026. What caused it, what went down, and what it means for how you design your infrastructure.

### Alon Shrestha
On May 7, 2026, a single data center in AWS's us-east-1 region got too hot. Servers shut themselves down. Power was lost. And for the next 28 hours, thousands of customers watched their infrastructure sit there, impaired, while AWS engineers worked to bring cooling systems back online.

## What Actually Happened
At 4:20 PM PDT on May 7, temperatures inside a single data center within availability zone use1-az4 exceeded safe operating thresholds.  They shut down immediately to protect the hardware.

# AWS Confirms Data Center Outage Caused By ‘Thermal Event,’ Some Services Still Impacted

“[AWS] began experiencing an increase in instance impairments within the affected zone due to the loss of power during a thermal event,” AWS said this morning. Here’s what you need to know about the AWS data center outage.

One of AWS’ busiest data centers suffered an outage Thursday night due to a “thermal event” with key AWS services like EC2 instance and EBS volumes still impacted as of Friday morning.

AWS confirmed the outage was due to overheating caused by a cooling failure at its North Virginia data center called US-EAST-1 region, which is a heavily used region.

On Thursday evening, AWS “began experiencing an increase in instance impairments within the affected zone due to the loss of power during a thermal event,” the company said Friday morning on its status report.

[Related: AWS CEO Says AI Not ‘Taking Away Jobs’ As Company Plans 11,000 Software Hires]

Key AWS services such as Amazon Redshift, Amazon SageMaker, ElastiCache, AWS IoT Core, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service and AWS Nat Gateway were impacted.

One of AWS newly minted technology partnerships—cryptocurrency exchange platform Coinbase—was impacted by the outage for roughly seven hours.

snippets:
# AWS Power Outage in Middle East Triggers Major Disruption to EC2 and Networking Services
A major power outage in the AWS me-central-1 (Middle East) region on March 1, 2026, resulted from an unusual physical incident where external objects struck a data center, triggering sparks and a fire.

## Mitigation and Partial Recovery
Despite the progress in restoring API functionality, the underlying physical infrastructure remained offline. AWS stated they were still awaiting clearance from local authorities to safely restore power to the damaged facility.

“We are still awaiting permission to turn the power back on, and once we have, we will ensure we restore power and connectivity safely,” an AWS representative stated in the 9:41 AM PST update.

# Power outage affects part of SF's Market Street after equipment damage
#### By Bay City News • Published July 4, 2026 • Updated on July 4, 2026 at 12:00 pm
About 90 Pacific Gas and Electric customers in San Francisco's Castro District were still without power on Saturday after a small outage struck a stretch of Market Street on Friday.

Traffic signals could be inoperable in the outage area, which included most of the 2200 block of Market Street and the blocks between Noe and Sanchez streets and from 15th to 16th streets, according to the San Francisco Department of Emergency Management.
